The Laptop Closed Itself

Rohan had the FAFSA open for four minutes. Then he hit a screen that said the form needed a “contributor,” closed the laptop, and went to go mow the Pattersons’ lawn instead.

I didn’t chase him. I’ve watched that exact moment happen at my counter. For sixteen years I ran the front office at a high school north of Austin, and every January brought a line of parents holding a form they’d half-filled and half-understood. The word that stops people cold isn’t usually a hard one. It’s an unfamiliar one. “Contributor” sounds like a summons. It isn’t.

Rohan needed to know who would have to answer with him. For our form, that included me. A contributor supplies their part of the form and, when required, gives consent and approval to use tax information and signs; Chapter 2 explains what that means. Nobody is being deposed.

What this form actually is

The FAFSA is long. It saves your progress. You do not have to finish in one sitting. When I helped families at school, some needed a break to check a number. Save a draft when you need to check a number. Before submitting, return to every required question, complete every contributor section and signature, and confirm the form was received. That’s normal. If a question makes you stop and stare at the screen, that’s not a sign you’re doing it wrong. It’s a sign the form is doing its job, which is asking for specific numbers instead of guesses.

The 2027-28 FAFSA form is live. StudentAid.gov says it uses 2025 tax information for attendance from July 1, 2027 through June 30, 2028. The 2027-28 handbook guidance is not yet published, so this book labels handbook rules 2026-27 and sends you to StudentAid.gov for current instructions.

The book follows the questions a family hits sitting at the table together. First, the accounts and the consent that let the form run at all. Then the questions that trip people up hardest: who counts as a parent when a marriage has ended, what a small business or a farm has to report, what counts as an asset and what doesn’t. Then what the form does with everything you’ve told it: the number it produces at the end, and what that number does and doesn’t mean. Only after that number exists do we get to the part nobody warns you about. That’s reading the award letter a school sends back, so a loan doesn’t get mistaken for a gift, and knowing when and how to ask a school to look again if your family’s situation has changed.

I’m not going to hand you a 2027-28 Pell Grant dollar figure, because the Department of Education hadn’t published one at the time I wrote this, and a guess printed in a book outlives the year it was wrong about. Where a number changes every year, or by state, or by school, I’ll tell you exactly where to go look it up yourself — StudentAid.gov, mostly, plus the agencies and offices named along the way. The form’s layout and rules can change. Check the current award-year form and instructions at StudentAid.gov before following any step-by-step guide.

The three things families get wrong most

After watching this process from the front office, and then again as a parent myself, I’ve come to believe almost every FAFSA headache traces back to one of three habits.

Waiting to make the accounts. Families treat the StudentAid.gov account as step three or four, something to get to after they’ve found the tax return and had the big conversation about who’s paying for what. Tonight is for starting, not solving every account problem. Chapter 1 owns the setup and repairs.

Treating consent as optional, or as a formality to click past. Somewhere in the form, every contributor has to consent to the IRS sending over tax information. It feels like paperwork. It is the single gate the entire application sits behind — skip it, and the form will not produce an aid number for your student, full stop, no matter how carefully everything else was filled in. I’ll explain exactly what you’re consenting to and why it matters this much in Chapter 2.

Reading “aid” on the award letter as if every line on it were a gift. A letter arrives from a school with a dollar figure at the top, and it’s easy to read the whole thing as money that’s simply yours. Some of it is. Some of it is a loan with your student’s name on it, or your name on it, that gets paid back with interest. Those are very different kinds of help, and the letters don’t always make the difference obvious. We’ll get to reading one line by line later in this book.

What this book doesn’t cover

I want to say this once, plainly, so you’re not waiting for it later: this book does not teach you how to save for college, or how to think about a 529 plan as an investment strategy. Chapter 5 explains when an education savings account is reported as an asset, including cases where the form does not ask for assets; this book does not teach investment strategy. If you’re looking for help building a college-savings strategy from scratch, that’s a different book than this one. What you’re holding is for the form that’s open on your screen right now, this year, with a deadline somewhere ahead of you.

When to call someone who isn’t me

I was the person at the front desk who could translate a form into plain English. I was never the person who could tell a family what to do with their tax return, their divorce decree, or their small business’s books, and I’m still not. I’ll tell you, plainly and by name, exactly when a chapter’s topic has crossed into territory that needs a professional. A CPA or tax preparer, when a business or a rental makes the numbers genuinely unclear. The school’s own financial aid office, for anything involving that school’s own money. A family law attorney, when a custody order and the form’s rules don’t seem to agree. The Federal Student Aid Information Center, when an account or an identity check gets stuck. The school’s financial aid office and federal aid help line are free; ask a CPA or attorney about fees before booking. They exist because this process has edge cases no single book can fully anticipate.

Tonight’s task

Make the StudentAid.gov accounts. Record account created, email confirmed, and any status the site shows. Stop there tonight.

Rohan came back from the Pattersons’ with grass clippings on his shoes and found me making my own StudentAid.gov login at the kitchen table, the one I’d need later as a contributor on his form. He watched for a second, then said, “that’s it?” That’s it. The rest of this book is just what comes after.

Chapter 1: Who Has to Answer, and How to Log In

Vikram made his account on a Tuesday night, typing fast because the baseball game was on in the other room. Where the form asked for his name, he typed “Vik.” Three days later his account sat at “needs action,” and neither of us could tell why until I made him read the error screen out loud.

That one word cost him a week. Let’s start before that mistake, not after it, so you don’t have to make it too.

What a contributor actually is

Under the 2026-27 Federal Student Aid Handbook’s Application and Verification Guide, a contributor is anyone required to provide information, consent and approval, and a signature on the FAFSA form. That includes the student. It includes at least one parent, if the student is a dependent. Sometimes it includes a parent’s spouse. The form is organized around this word — each contributor gets their own section, their own login, their own set of questions about their own finances. Nobody answers for anybody else.

I want to be honest about why that word lands so badly on first contact. “Contributor” sounds like something from a deposition, or a tax form you’d need a lawyer to read. It’s doing a narrower job than that. It’s naming, plainly, who has to show up and answer, as opposed to who simply cares about the outcome. A grandparent who’s helping pay tuition isn’t a contributor unless the form specifically requires it of them. A sibling isn’t one. The question the form is actually asking, under all that formality, is “whose numbers do we need.”

That distinction matters because of what each contributor’s section asks for. It isn’t a general background check. It’s a request for that one person’s specific financial facts — income, tax filing status, certain assets — the same facts you’d expect a tax preparer to ask for, not a character reference. Knowing that in advance takes some of the sting out of the word the first time it shows up on a screen.

The reason the Department moved away from just saying “parent” is that FAFSA households don’t sort into that one word anymore. A stepparent who didn’t adopt the student might still have to answer. An ex-spouse who hasn’t lived in the house for six years might not. “Contributor” is a wider net that catches the right people regardless of what the household looks like, and Chapter 3 walks through exactly how the form decides which parent that is when parents are divorced or never married. For now, hold onto the simple version: a contributor is anyone the form requires an answer from, and each one answers for themselves.

Making the accounts

Before anyone can contribute anything, they need a StudentAid.gov account. This is the part people put off, because it feels like paperwork before the paperwork, and it’s also the part that causes the most avoidable delay if you wait.

Each contributor needs their own account: their own email address, their own username and password, never shared with anyone else in the household. Use your own StudentAid.gov account to open your section. After answering, follow the form’s separate instructions to acknowledge its terms, electronically sign your section and submit it. Chapter 2 distinguishes that signature from tax-information consent.

That order is set out on the Department’s current “Filling Out the FAFSA Form” page, and it repays a second reading, because the word “submit” does two different jobs there. You submit your own section. The form itself isn’t finished until every required contributor has completed theirs, given the tax-information permission and signed. One person racing ahead doesn’t move the application along by itself. It just means the waiting starts somewhere else.

This is also why one shared family email address causes so much trouble. If Rohan and I had both tried to use the same inbox, StudentAid.gov would have no way to tell our two accounts apart, and neither of us would be able to prove, later, that the answers under our section were ours. If you need a separate email address, create a free one that only that contributor controls. Fifteen minutes, one contributor, done — except it often isn’t done in fifteen minutes, because of what happened to Vikram.

The name-match trap

The student’s name, date of birth and Social Security number get checked against Social Security Administration records as part of making the account and filing the form. That check is strict, and it is not looking for the name people actually go by. It’s looking for the name on the card.

One qualification before the story, because it decides whether this section applies to a given person at all. If the contributor has an SSN, enter the name matching SSA’s record. If not, follow StudentAid.gov’s account and identity-verification instructions for contributors without an SSN. The account page itself hedges the same way — it asks for your name as it appears on your Social Security card if you have one, and for an SSN if you have one. Parents and spouses without Social Security numbers are expected to show up on this form, and the identity route for them is spelled out on the site rather than in this book.

Vikram goes by Vik everywhere except his passport and his Social Security card, where he’s Vikram. He typed “Vik” into the account, because that’s who he is to every person who knows him. The system flagged it, because Social Security has never heard of a Vik.

Here’s the part worth knowing before it happens to you: there are two different reasons this match can fail, and they need two different fixes. Ask yourself which one you’re looking at before you touch anything.

Branch A: Social Security’s own record is wrong. Maybe there was a legal name change after a marriage or a court order. The update never made it into SSA’s system, even though everything the family typed into the FAFSA is correct and current. In that case, the fix starts with SSA, not with StudentAid.gov. Correct the record directly with the Social Security Administration, and wait for their confirmation that it’s updated. From there you have two paths: ask the Federal Student Aid Information Center to manually resync the data with SSA, or ask the school to help. A school can set the record to resend for matching through its own systems and submit the fix as a correction.

Branch B: what got typed into the FAFSA was wrong. This was Vikram’s branch. The name on his Social Security card was never the problem; “Vik” was a shortcut he typed without thinking about what the form would do with it. For this branch, the fix lives entirely on StudentAid.gov: log in, go to Account Settings, correct the name so it matches the Social Security card exactly, and that correction gets automatically resent to SSA for a fresh match. Once SSA verifies it, submit a FAFSA correction so the application reflects the fixed account.

Ask the one-sentence question before you do anything else: is SSA’s record wrong, or is what we typed wrong? Branch A starts with a phone call to Social Security. Branch B starts with Account Settings on StudentAid.gov. Guess wrong, and you’ll spend a week waiting on the wrong fix. That’s roughly what happened to us before I made Vikram read the actual error text instead of assuming.

Vikram’s fix took four days once he knew which branch he was on: Account Settings, the full legal name, a resubmitted match, a FAFSA correction. If your family hits this and you’re not sure which branch applies, or the status doesn’t clear the way you’d expect, that uncertainty is worth a direct question to the people who run the system, not another guess.

The one case with no fix on this side of the form

There’s a narrower problem worth knowing about even if it doesn’t apply to your family. For 2026-27, most students applying for Title IV aid needed an SSN, but citizens of a Freely Associated State had a special no-SSN route, including online account verification. A paper application without a student SSN was returned unprocessed outside that exception. Check StudentAid.gov or the Federal Student Aid Information Center for your 2027-28 filing route before assuming you cannot file online.

I’m being this careful because the stakes of getting it wrong run in one direction. A family that wrongly believes the door is shut doesn’t file at all, and nobody follows up with them. Ask first.

What the live 2027-28 form actually shows

Here’s what I can tell you for certain, checked directly against StudentAid.gov: the 2027-28 FAFSA form is live. It asks for 2025 tax information. Its attendance period begins July 1, 2027 and ends June 30, 2028. That much I verified on the site itself, not in a handbook, because the handbook for 2027-28 hadn’t published a single guide page as of this writing.

So here’s the honest line between the two. These account and correction mechanics come from the 2026-27 handbook. Before using them for the live 2027-28 application, follow its current StudentAid.gov instructions or ask the Federal Student Aid Information Center.

I’d rather say that twelve times in this book than let you read a handbook sentence as settled law for a cycle it was never written for.

Doing this together, at one table

The best version of this step that I’ve seen — in my own kitchen and at the front counter for sixteen years — involves one table and one laptop passed between people. Keep the 2025 tax return available if the live 2027-28 form asks for figures you cannot confirm without it; StudentAid.gov says most families can start without gathering documents. The form saves as you go. That’s not a consolation prize; it’s the actual design. You are not expected to finish the account step and the whole application in one sitting, and trying to force that usually produces the kind of rushed typing that got Vikram’s name wrong in the first place.

Turn the introduction’s brief account notes into a card for each required contributor. Record the person’s name, their own email, whether the account was created and email confirmed, and the identity status shown by StudentAid.gov. Leave passwords and Social Security numbers off the card. Add one question if a match fails: “Is SSA’s record wrong, or did we enter the wrong information?” Record which branch applies, the contact or correction made, and when you’ll recheck identity status.

The repair entries build on the brief notes you started tonight. The point isn’t more paperwork. It’s that a week from now, when somebody asks what you already tried, you can answer from the card instead of from memory. Memory is where these repairs go to die — one person thinks the call was made, another thinks the correction was submitted, and nobody rechecks.

When to call someone

If Account Settings won’t accept a correction, call the Federal Student Aid Information Center. If SSA has confirmed a change but it has not reached your application, ask the Center or your school about a new match. Don’t invent a third repair path.

The Center can see your account from the inside in a way no checklist can replace. A school is different: it can help with the resend step in Branch A, but it has no window into your personal account settings. Knowing which of the two to call saves a day on its own.

What to expect once the accounts are made

Once every contributor’s account shows a verified identity status, nothing dramatic happens next. Nobody gets an email congratulating them. The account simply sits there, ready, until the next contributor logs in to start their section of the form. That quiet is part of why families underestimate this step: it doesn’t feel like progress, because there’s nothing to point at yet.

Which is exactly why you check instead of assume. Check each required contributor’s account and identity status in StudentAid.gov. Record any outstanding action; don’t assume a successful login means the account is verified.

Resist the urge to treat a verified account as license to rush through everything else at the same pace. The account step rewards care precisely because it’s slow and checkable. Every later step — the tax-information consent in Chapter 2, the parent and dependency questions in later chapters — builds on these accounts being correct. A name typed wrong here doesn’t just cost a week fixing the account; it can delay every contributor’s section behind it, because the form won’t finish processing a signature tied to an unverified identity.

Treat the account step the way you’d treat laying a foundation: unglamorous, invisible once the rest of the house goes up, and the one place where a mistake is hardest to see until much later.

Make the accounts tonight if you haven’t already, each one under the name SSA has on file for that person — or, where there’s no SSN, under whatever the site’s own identity route tells you to enter. Everything after this chapter — the consent screen, the parent question, the assets — assumes those accounts already exist and already match.

Chapter 2: The Consent Screen, and What the SAI Actually Is

Vikram had pushed his chair back from the kitchen table. Rohan was still leaning toward the laptop, waiting for a number that wasn’t coming.

“I did my part,” Vikram said.

He’d answered the questions he understood. He’d left the tax-information permission alone because he wanted to read it properly, then forgot to return. On that application he was a required contributor. His unfinished permission mattered just as much as the answers he’d carefully entered.

Rohan thought he’d broken something. Vikram thought the website was slow. I reached for the yellow pad beside the fruit bowl and wrote their names on separate lines. Beside each name: permission, signature, section complete. We needed to find the missing action, not keep refreshing.

This was our consent stumble, not a claim about a particular button or error message on your form. Public FAFSA guidance for the live form confirms that all required contributors must complete their sections, give consent and approval, and sign. Its consent instructions are usable now. I haven’t verified the wording or position of buttons inside your signed-in application, so I won’t invent a click sequence.

The administrative source below is the Application and Verification Guide, 2026-27 edition, within the Federal Student Aid Handbook. Check StudentAid.gov for your current cycle’s instructions; an older handbook is not proof of next year’s rule.

The pipe between the IRS and the form

FA-DDX. FUTURE Act Direct Data Exchange. An awkward name for a connection between the Internal Revenue Service and Federal Student Aid, part of the Department of Education.

The IRS holds federal tax information. The exchange lets the Department request specified information and use it in the aid application. You aren’t uploading your whole tax folder to a stranger who offered to help.

FTI means federal tax information. I’ll use “tax information” where that will do.

According to the 2026-27 guide’s chapter “Filling Out the FAFSA Form,” this exchange can supply income and tax information directly from the IRS. Tax information successfully transferred through it is considered verified for federal student aid purposes. It doesn’t mean every answer elsewhere on the application has been checked.

The Department’s live filing guidance also explains an initially unsettling feature: the transferred federal tax information won’t display on the FAFSA site or the FAFSA Submission Summary. You may not get a familiar screen full of tax-return amounts to inspect.

That absence isn’t, by itself, evidence of a failed transfer.

Under the 2026-27 handbook, students and contributors cannot view or edit the imported information; the school’s financial aid administrator can see it on the school’s application record. If you believe something is wrong, identify the concern and ask the aid office how to resolve it. Don’t invent replacement amounts because you can’t see the imported ones.

I like automatic entry when it saves someone from copying the wrong line. I don’t like “automatic” being used to mean “nothing else to do.” Follow the questions and help instructions the current form actually gives you. A tax transfer isn’t the whole application.

What the permission actually permits

The permission has two directions. Your identifying information goes to the IRS so it can find the relevant record. Tax information comes back to the Department so it can evaluate student aid eligibility.

The 2026-27 guide distinguishes consent from approval. Consent permits the use and disclosure of identifying information for the IRS match. Approval permits the Department to receive, use and redisclose federal tax information for the authorized aid purposes.

Redisclose means share onward under those rules.

The same 2026-27 source names eligible institutions, state higher education agencies and designated scholarship organizations as authorized recipients for aid administration. This isn’t permission for unrestricted public sharing.

For the available 2027-28 application, StudentAid.gov’s current filling-out guidance describes the permission in plain terms. It includes matching identifying information with IRS records, receiving tax information, using it to determine aid eligibility and sharing it with schools and state higher education agencies. It also describes reuse on another student’s FAFSA, such as when a parent contributes for another child.

Read the actual statement in your application. The explanation here helps you understand it; it doesn’t replace it.

Here’s the sentence I most want you to carry away: Under the 2026-27 handbook, a student is ineligible for Title IV aid while any required contributor’s tax-information approval is missing.

Title IV is the federal student aid covered by that law, not a promise about every private scholarship. This missing permission isn’t merely a preference about convenient data entry.

The current StudentAid.gov instructions likewise say that a required spouse or parent who declines the transfer permission prevents federal student aid eligibility. Typing tax information field by field does not get around that requirement.

You can pause to understand a permission. You cannot treat the pause as completion.

No tax return doesn’t mean no consent

The live Department guidance explicitly addresses contributors who didn’t file taxes, filed outside the United States or don’t have a Social Security number. They still need to provide consent and approval.

It can feel illogical to authorize a search when you expect the search to find no return. But “there is no return to retrieve” and “I haven’t authorized retrieval” are different facts. Don’t substitute one for the other.

The 2026-27 handbook requires the applicant and every applicable contributor to give the permission regardless of filing method. Paper is not a consent-free alternative. Nor does the student’s approval cover a parent’s missing approval.

Use the contributor list from Chapter 1 rather than adding everyone in the household. The question here is whether each person who is actually required has completed this action. Choosing the correct parent in a separated family belongs to Chapter 3.

At our table, the yellow pad exposed what the phrase “I did my part” concealed. Rohan’s action couldn’t finish Vikram’s. My knowing the household’s tax information couldn’t finish it either. Vikram had to return to the Department’s process himself, read the permission and supply his own response.

A cycle is not a calendar year

According to the 2026-27 application guide, consent and approval are given once for that FAFSA cycle and cannot be revoked for that cycle. A new cycle requires its own permission.

Read that before agreeing. I won’t describe an irreversible permission as a harmless box to click past.

The cycle is the application period associated with a particular FAFSA award year. It isn’t simply January through December, and it isn’t the tax year printed on a return.

The handbook illustrates this with the 2026-27 FAFSA cycle, which it describes as running from August 2025 to September 2027. Those dates are its example of a cycle’s length. They are not the 2027-28 cycle dates, not your school’s priority deadline and not advice to wait until September.

For the current window, check StudentAid.gov. Don’t move the example dates forward a year and call that research.

Keep the cycle label beside your consent record. A note saying “approved last fall” becomes ambiguous when another application opens. A note naming the FAFSA year tells you which application the action belongs to.

Consent and signature do different jobs

Consent and approval authorize the tax-information process. A signature certifies the application information. Completing either one doesn’t establish that you’ve completed the other.

The 2026-27 guide explains why this matters after filing. A correction can require another signature even though the contributor already gave consent and approval for that cycle. The correction needs certification; the existing cycle permission doesn’t need to be collected again.

If a notice says a signature is missing, read it as a signature problem. Don’t assume the tax permission failed. Equally, a signed page doesn’t necessarily establish that the required tax approval exists.

That dated handbook also draws a firm boundary around helpers. Only the Department may collect consent and approval for this tax-information use. A school can help resolve a missing signature through the permitted process, but collecting that signature doesn’t satisfy missing consent.

A counselor can explain a sentence. An advocate can sit beside you. One parent can remind another. None of them can supply the other contributor’s consent on their behalf.

For your live application, check StudentAid.gov rather than looking for a button described in an older guide. The Department’s current filing page says completion requires all required contributors to finish their sections, provide consent and approval, and sign. Finishing your own section is not necessarily finishing the family’s form.

When the IRS cannot supply usable data

A failed retrieval isn’t the same as a refusal to consent. Under the 2026-27 rules, an approved request can still produce no usable tax data.

The handbook describes IRS response codes on the ISIR, the Institutional Student Information Record. That’s the application record used by the school. These are not code labels I’m claiming you’ll see on a 2027-28 parent screen.

In the 2026-27 guide, code 200 means usable federal tax information was retrieved. Code 214 means the IRS located the individual but found no return on file for the relevant tax year. Codes 203, 206 and 212 mean the IRS could not provide usable information.

You don’t need to memorize them. Knowing that the school has a record of the response lets you ask a more useful question than “Why is FAFSA broken?”

For the last group of codes, the 2026-27 guide requires that contributor to enter income and tax information manually. Those entries are used in calculating the Student Aid Index, but they are not considered verified merely because someone typed them. The Department or institution may require verification if the application is selected.

Manual entry is a route for supplying needed information when retrieval doesn’t provide it. It isn’t a route around required consent, and it isn’t permission to guess.

Follow the current form’s request and its tax-year instructions. If it asks for information you can’t confidently identify, stop at that question and obtain the proper record or help. Don’t interpret “no return on file” as proof that no filing obligation existed; ask a qualified tax preparer if that is genuinely uncertain.

Call the school’s financial aid office when a retrieval problem, a manual-entry request or a verification notice leaves you unsure what documentation is needed. The office can inspect the school’s record and explain its requirements. I cannot see those records from your kitchen table.

A useful opening is: “We’re working on the 2027-28 FAFSA. This contributor supplied consent, but we’re being asked for tax information manually. What should we check, and what documents do you need?”

Give the exact message if you have one. Send sensitive documents only through the secure method that office specifies. A pile of tax pages attached to an ordinary email is not my version of getting organized.

The SAI is not an invoice

SAI. Student Aid Index. A number, not a bill.

StudentAid.gov’s “What is the Student Aid Index?” explanation, checked on October 5, 2026, calls it an eligibility index used by a school’s financial aid office. It results from the information on the FAFSA.

The Department expressly distinguishes it from the aid amount you’ll receive, the amount your family is expected to provide and the final financial aid offer.

According to Federal Student Aid’s implementation letter GEN-23-11, the SAI replaced the Expected Family Contribution, or EFC. If an older handout uses that term, don’t treat the old label as a current instruction to pay.

An index doesn’t know whether your student has chosen a school. It isn’t that school’s invoice. When you eventually see it, keep its label attached. Don’t copy it into the household budget under “tuition owed.”

Chapter 7 explains the calculation and Pell eligibility. There is no guessed 2027-28 Pell amount here and no borrowed handbook example dressed up as your award. Check StudentAid.gov for the current award-year information. The school’s actual aid offer is a later document; Chapter 9 handles reading it.

For now, the useful distinction is between a missing action and a number you don’t like. A missing consent needs that contributor’s action. Disliking an index doesn’t tell you which answer, if any, is wrong.

The consent checklist, without tax amounts

Make one entry per required contributor for this FAFSA cycle. Leave passwords, Social Security numbers and tax figures off this working sheet.

  1. Write the contributor’s name and FAFSA cycle.
  2. Record whether consent and approval were provided: yes, no or not yet confirmed. Add the date the contributor confirms the action.
  3. Record the signature separately, then whether the required section is complete. Don’t infer either from the consent entry.
  4. For anything unresolved, write the exact action or question, who must handle it and when you’ll check again.

On our pad, Vikram’s entry first said “consent: no; return and read permission.” Rohan’s said “consent: yes.” We didn’t add tax amounts to prove those entries. We needed to locate an unfinished task, not recreate the return.

Choose a check-in time you can keep. It is your reminder, not an official processing deadline. If the current form gives different instructions or an action-required notice, follow those instructions instead.

Put the pad beside the laptop. Ask each required contributor about their own line.

Chapter 3: Divorced, Separated, Never Married

Gabe kept a custody calendar on the refrigerator. The children spent more nights at their mother’s house, so he assumed she would be the parent on the FAFSA. It sounded settled. It wasn’t.

The form does not use a calendar of overnight stays to choose between divorced parents. The Department’s 2026-27 Application and Verification Guide assigns the parent role according to who provided more than half of the student’s financial support during the preceding 12 months. That parent may not be the one the student lived with most. This is the 2026-27 rule; check StudentAid.gov for the instructions that apply to the live 2027-28 application. The form is available, but the matching handbook guidance has not been published as of October 5, 2026. I won’t pretend a past-year rule is a confirmed future-year rule.

That distinction is the whole chapter. Residence tells you where the student slept. Support asks who paid more of the student’s support over the period the handbook specifies. A parenting plan, a school address, and the name on a custody order may be relevant to your family, but they do not replace that federal test.

Start with the right question

When a student is dependent for federal aid purposes and the legal parents are divorced, separated, or never married and do not live together, the 2026-27 guidance measures financial support, not custody. The parent above the halfway mark in that 12-month period is the one whose information goes on the form. StudentAid.gov’s public parent-information page describes the distinction too. The page does not replace the missing 2027-28 handbook, so check the current instructions before using the rule to complete this year’s application.

“More than 50%” means more than half, not exactly half. If you reach an equal split, neither parent provided more than half. The 2026-27 Handbook says that if neither parent provided more than half, the parent with the greater income and assets is the contributor. If neither parent supported the student financially, the same greater-income-and-assets fallback applies. Again: that is the 2026-27 rule. Confirm the current instructions rather than carrying it forward by instinct.

The comparison covers the last 12 months, not the parents’ entire history. A divorce finalized years ago does not settle this year’s support comparison. Neither does a parent’s old tax return, a past child-support arrangement, or a pattern from the previous school year. Build the answer from the period the applicable instructions name.

The form’s live 2027-28 materials also make one timing point plain: marital status is reported as of the day the FAFSA is filled out or signed, not projected into the future. StudentAid.gov’s 2027-28 filling-out guidance, checked October 5, 2026, says the form asks for current marital status and directs families whose status changed since the tax return to its current instructions. Don’t mark “divorced” because a divorce is expected next month, or “married” because you hope to reconcile. Answer the question as it stands on the date the form asks you to answer it.

Make a support record, not a custody argument

Parents often arrive with different kinds of proof. One has the calendar. The other has bank statements. One remembers paying for the braces; the other remembers the monthly transfer. Start by laying out the same 12-month period for both parents, using the date range stated by the current StudentAid.gov instructions. Don’t silently substitute a calendar year or a school year.

Make a private worksheet with one column for each parent. List the support payments you can identify and document: direct payments for the student’s needs, transfers, and amounts paid under an arrangement such as child support. If a bill was shared, write down how you assigned each parent’s part. If one payment appears in more than one record, count it once. The worksheet is a way to make your comparison legible; it is not a Department worksheet or a substitute for the official instructions.

For 2026-27, the Department’s Application and Verification Guide says child support and alimony paid count on the payer’s side of this comparison. That can surprise a parent who thinks of a transfer only as money arriving in another household. Record it once, not once as a payment and again as a shared bill. This is not confirmed for 2027-28; verify the current instructions before making the comparison.

Write down what you know and what you don’t. A canceled check, payment history, receipt, or shared-expense record can make a disputed figure easier to discuss. Don’t invent precision where the records won’t support it. The goal is a good-faith comparison under the official rule, not a spreadsheet that looks impressive.

Keep the notes plain enough that another adult could follow them. Put the date range at the top. For each entry, record the amount, who paid it, what it covered, and where you found the record. If a payment covered several people in the household, don’t assign the entire amount to the student without a basis. Mark the uncertainty and ask the aid office how it wants that situation documented. The public summary of the rule does not provide a complete household-accounting method, so this worksheet should organize evidence, not manufacture a formula.

You do not need to turn this into a courtroom exhibit before you can ask a question. A short, dated list and copies of the records that support it are often easier for an aid office to review than a long argument about which parent did more. Keep private financial documents secure, and send them only through a method the school confirms. If the other parent will not share records, write down what you have and what remains unknown rather than filling the gap with a guess.

The support-test worksheet

  1. Confirm which parent situations the current StudentAid.gov instructions cover and the exact 12-month period they specify.
  2. For each parent, list support you can identify for that same period. Note the source for each entry.
  3. Include child support and alimony paid on the payer’s side when applying the 2026-27 Handbook rule; check StudentAid.gov for 2027-28 treatment.
  4. Compare the two totals. If one parent provided more than half, the 2026-27 rule points to that parent. If the totals are equal, or neither parent provided more than half, the 2026-27 fallback compares income and assets.
  5. Save the records and the method you used. If the result depends on a disputed legal or financial fact, pause and ask the school’s financial aid office what documentation it needs.

That final step matters. A worksheet can organize facts. It cannot decide a contested legal question for you.

Why the nights can point the wrong way

Gabe’s custody calendar showed the children at their mother’s home most nights. He thought that made her the FAFSA parent. When he compared the financial support each parent had provided during the period named in the 2026-27 instructions, the result was different from the calendar. His first answer had been tidy. It was also based on the wrong measure.

The point isn’t that overnight stays never matter in family life. They matter a great deal there. The point is that the federal form’s parent test is not a custody test. If the student sleeps at one home and the other parent pays a larger share of support, the support rule can point to the second parent. If that feels counterintuitive, return to the exact question: who provided more than half of the support in the applicable period?

Do not let a decree answer a question it was not written to answer. A custody order may establish parenting time or support obligations. It does not, by itself, decide which parent meets the federal aid test. The 2026-27 Handbook names support as the deciding measure. Check the current StudentAid.gov guidance for 2027-28 before you file, especially if your circumstances do not fit the plain example.

The second household can matter too

The parent selected under the support test may have remarried. That does not make the new spouse the student’s legal parent, and a stepparent who has not adopted the student cannot stand in as the only parent. But the 2026-27 Handbook says a parent’s spouse may still be required to provide information in certain situations. It identifies a remarried parent who did not file a joint tax return with the current spouse for the base year, and an unmarried parent living with the student’s other legal parent. Those are 2026-27 handbook rules; check StudentAid.gov for the live year’s directions.

This is where families can get tangled: “Who is my parent?” and “Who else must contribute?” are related questions, but not the same one. First identify the parent under the applicable rule. Then follow the form’s prompts about that parent’s current spouse or household. Don’t invite every adult who has ever helped with a bill, and don’t leave out a person just because they are not the student’s biological parent. Use the StudentAid.gov “Who’s My FAFSA Parent?” tool and the current parent-information instructions when the household does not fit a simple two-home picture.

If the parents were never married to each other but live together, the 2026-27 Handbook says both biological or adoptive parents provide information. A household can be unmarried and still be one shared household for this purpose. “Never married” alone does not tell you to choose one parent. The living arrangement matters under that year’s guidance. Confirm the live 2027-28 instructions before applying this detail.

If one parent has died, the 2026-27 Handbook says the student remains dependent on the surviving biological or adoptive parent, rather than a stepparent who supports the student, unless that stepparent adopted them. The handbook also says a grandparent or other relative raising a student is not a parent for this purpose unless the relative adopted the student. These are sensitive situations, and I won’t flatten them into a quick rule for 2027-28 without its published handbook. Check StudentAid.gov and contact the school’s financial aid office if the student’s legal relationship or family history makes the answer unclear.

When the answer is disputed

Sometimes the parents disagree about the amount of support. Sometimes the legal documents use “custodial parent” in a way that sounds decisive. Sometimes an agreement says one parent is responsible for expenses while the records show a different pattern. These are not reasons to choose the answer that feels fairest, or to let the student referee a dispute between adults.

Use the current StudentAid.gov guidance first, then bring the records and the exact point of disagreement to the school’s financial aid office. The office can explain what documentation it needs to process the application. It cannot rewrite a family-law order, and this book cannot interpret one. If a decree, support order, or contested payment obligation is central to the answer, speak with a family law attorney about the legal document and a tax or financial professional only if the records themselves need help. The FAFSA question remains governed by the current federal instructions; the attorney’s role is to explain your legal situation, not to invent a different federal test.

There is a practical line between uncertainty and a legal dispute. If the parents simply need to assemble receipts and agree on arithmetic, do that together if it is safe and workable. If they disagree about what an order requires, whether a transfer was support, or what the records mean, don’t ask the student to settle it at the kitchen table. Get the school’s written guidance about the FAFSA documentation, and professional legal advice about the order.

The date on the form is not a prediction

Marital status can change between a tax return and the day the FAFSA is completed. The live 2027-28 StudentAid.gov guidance, checked October 5, 2026, says to report current marital status as of the date the form is filled out, and points to year-specific instructions when a parent’s status changed since the tax filing. That is what the public 2027-28 guidance verifies; don’t infer other form screens or unpublished handbook rules from it.

If a wedding, separation, or divorce is pending, don’t answer based on the expected outcome. If the change already happened, don’t assume the old tax return’s filing status controls the current marital-status answer. Those facts may create separate questions about how financial information is entered. Chapter 2 covers consent and tax-data mechanics; this chapter stays with who is a parent and how the support test works. Follow the current 2027-28 help page for the changed-status situation, and ask the aid office before submitting if the instructions still don’t fit.

Here’s the move. Write down the period you’re comparing, list each parent’s support from records, and check the live StudentAid.gov parent guidance before deciding who to invite. Ten minutes to make the worksheet. More time if the records need it. If a custody order is colliding with the support rule, call a family law attorney instead of asking your student to pick a side.

Chapter 4: The Business and Farm Questions That Changed

Gabe caught me at the end of the driveway with a shoebox under one arm and a look I’ve seen across a front counter a hundred times.

“They count my business now,” he said. “Somebody at the ballfield told me they count the business.”

The box held invoices. Three years of them, rubber-banded by season, because he’d decided the only way to survive this question was to bring everything.

I asked him one thing first. Not what the trucks were worth. Not what he cleared last year.

“Who owns it, and how many people work for you?”

He blinked. “Me. And four guys, five in the spring.”

“Then put the box down.”

What actually changed, and when

Here’s the part the ballfield rumor got half right. Something did change.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act changed which businesses and farms have to be reported on the FAFSA, and the change took effect starting with the 2026-27 cycle. That’s the Federal Student Aid Handbook’s own framing of it, in the 2026-27 Application and Verification Guide, Chapter 2. Under that guidance, applicants report the net worth of a family business with more than 100 full-time or full-time-equivalent employees, and the net worth of a farm the family does not live on.

Read that twice, because the rumor almost always drops the numbers.

The same 2026-27 guidance lists what stays off the form. A family business with 100 or fewer full-time or full-time-equivalent employees that the family owns and controls. A farm where the family resides. A commercial fishing business owned and controlled by the family, along with its related expenses.

Gabe’s landscaping company has five people in it during the busy months, counting Gabe. He owns it outright. Nobody else has a say in how it runs. Under the 2026-27 rules, that business is excluded, and the shoebox stays in his truck.

I need to be straight with you about something before we go further. I’m writing this while the 2026-27 handbook is the newest full edition the Department has published. The 2027-28 Application and Verification Guide wasn’t out yet. So every rule in this chapter carries the year it came from. Before you answer the business or farm question on your student’s form, check StudentAid.gov and the published guidance for your own award year. The form being live, as Chapter 1 confirmed, is not the same thing as published guidance explaining every rule behind it.

Don’t let anyone, including me, tell you a prior year’s threshold “will” hold. Look it up.

Why the old advice is half wrong, and the new rumor is worse

For years the shorthand was simple: small business, doesn’t count, move on. Parents repeated it. Counselors repeated it. It was close enough to true that nobody got hurt.

Then the law moved, and the shorthand flipped in the other direction. Now the ballfield version is “they count businesses,” which sends a man with four employees to the mailbox holding three years of invoices he doesn’t need.

Both versions skip the actual work, which is small. The exclusion didn’t vanish. What changed is that it now rests on conditions a family has to check instead of assume: the employee count, and whether the family both owns and controls the thing. Two questions. Neither one takes an accountant to ask, though one of them can take an accountant to answer precisely.

Gabe’s reaction is the one I want you to copy. Not the panic — the next part. He didn’t report the business because somebody said to. He didn’t skip it because somebody else said to. He checked the two tests, found he was excluded, and could say out loud why. If his form ever gets a second look from a school, he can explain his answer in one sentence. That’s the whole goal here.

The two tests, in the order to ask them

Do we own and control it? The 2026-27 guidance ties the exclusion to a business the family owns and controls, which means more than holding a piece of paper with your name on it. If you’re a minority partner in a company run by people you’re not related to, or you hold shares in something you have no say over, you’re outside what that exclusion describes. That’s not a small business in the handbook’s sense; that’s an investment, and investments are Chapter 5’s territory.

Where this gets murky is the middle ground. Family partnerships with cousins. An LLC where your brother-in-law holds forty percent. A business where your name is on the registration and your ex-spouse signs the checks. If you read “owned and controlled by the family” and genuinely can’t tell whether that describes your situation, that’s your signal to stop guessing. More on who to ask in a minute.

One wrinkle worth naming: “the family” here means the people whose information goes on this form, which is not always the people you’d list at Thanksgiving. If the contributor on your student’s form is one parent rather than two — the support test from Chapter 3 decides that — then the ownership question gets asked about that household, not about everyone related by blood. A business owned entirely by a parent who isn’t a contributor on this form isn’t that contributor’s asset to report. This is exactly the kind of tangle where an hour with the person who does the business’s taxes saves you a bad answer.

How many full-time or full-time-equivalent employees? The 2026-27 handbook sets the line at more than 100 for reporting, 100 or fewer for the exclusion. If you have four employees, or nine, or thirty-one, you are nowhere near the line and you can stop counting.

If you’re somewhere close to 100, that phrase “full-time-equivalent” is doing real work and you shouldn’t improvise it. Part-time hours get combined into equivalents under rules that don’t live on StudentAid.gov. The person who prepares your business’s taxes already deals with employee counts for other federal purposes and is the right person to ask how yours comes out.

For a farm: do you live on it? The 2026-27 guidance excludes a farm on which the family resides and requires reporting a farm the family does not reside on. Families who farm one place and live in town are the ones this catches. If you inherited a half-section two counties over and nobody in your household sleeps there, that is not the same answer as the home place.

Commercial fishing? The 2026-27 guidance names commercial fishing businesses owned and controlled by the family, and the related expenses, as excluded. If that’s your family, read the current year’s guidance directly rather than taking my paragraph for it.

If you do have to report it, what the number means

Say the tests come out the other way and the business or the farm belongs on the form. The amount you enter is net worth, and the 2026-27 guidance defines that for investments the same way throughout: current market value minus the debt owed on it. If the result is negative, you report zero. The form does not want a loss, and you don’t get credit for one.

Current market value is not what you paid. It is not the depreciated figure on a tax schedule. It is what the thing is worth right now, as of the day the form is signed, which is the point where guessing turns expensive in both directions.

Guess high and you hand the formula money your family doesn’t have. Guess low and you’ve put a wrong number on a federal application your student signed. Neither one is where you want to be in April.

Debt means debt against that specific thing. The mortgage on the farmland comes off the farmland’s market value. The note on the skid steer comes off the business. A credit card you’ve been living on, or the loan against your house, does not belong in this subtraction just because the money eventually went into the business. Keep the arithmetic attached to the asset.

And a reminder that saves families real money: the form asks for a snapshot. Net worth as of the day the application is signed, not an average, not last December. If the farmland is worth less this spring than it was last fall, the number you enter is this spring’s, with the documentation to match.

The call to make

This is the chapter where I stop being useful, and I’d rather say so than pretend.

Valuing a business or a farm is a professional job. Not a kitchen-table job, not a Saturday-morning-with-a-spreadsheet job. If your answer to the two tests is “report it,” or if your answer is “I honestly can’t tell,” call the CPA or the tax preparer who already does the business’s or the farm’s returns. They have the balance sheet, the depreciation schedules, the loan balances and the employee counts in front of them. Ask them for a current market value and the outstanding debt against it, in writing, with the date they prepared it. Ask what they charge first; this is paid help, unlike the school’s aid office.

Keep that document. If the form gets selected for review, a dated valuation from the person who does your books is a far better answer than your memory of a conversation.

And if the question is legal rather than financial — whose business it even is, after a divorce or a death — that’s an attorney’s question, not your tax preparer’s.

What if you already answered, and now you think you got it wrong? Don’t sit on it. A submitted FAFSA can be corrected, and a parent who reported a business that the guidance excludes has been handing the formula an asset the family shouldn’t have been charged for. Go back into the form on StudentAid.gov, fix the answer, and resubmit. If you can’t work out how, call the school’s financial aid office before you start clicking. That office sees corrections every week, it’s free, and it would rather talk you through one now than untangle it after an offer goes out.

The same goes in the other direction, and it’s the less comfortable conversation. If you suspect you omitted an asset, check the 2027-28 form’s current guidance and ask the school’s aid office what correction is needed; the farm-residence and employee-count examples above come from 2026-27, not confirmed 2027-28 guidance. A correction you made is a different thing entirely from an error a school found.

What else stays off, regardless

While we’re in the exclusions, the 2026-27 guidance also keeps several things off the asset question entirely, and these come up constantly whenever a family starts inventorying what they own.

Personal possessions. The family’s principal place of residence — the house you live in. Retirement plans: 401(k)s, pension funds, annuities, non-education IRAs, Keogh plans. The cash value or equity of whole life insurance. ABLE accounts.

One catch inside that list, and it’s the one people trip over: distributions from retirement plans do count as income under the same 2026-27 guidance. The account balance is excluded. Money you pulled out of it is not. If you took a withdrawal in the tax year the form uses, it is in your tax data and it will show up.

Chapter 5 takes the rest of the asset questions, including education savings accounts and rental property, and covers the circumstance where a family isn’t asked about assets at all. Don’t pre-answer those here.

The business and farm test

Apply this four-question test only to the 2026-27 handbook rules described above; before answering a 2027-28 FAFSA business or farm question, use the current StudentAid.gov form help and obtain school guidance for any uncertain ownership or valuation. Under 2026-27 guidance, the answers were:

  1. Do we own and control this business? If no, it isn’t covered by the small-business exclusion — treat it as an investment and see Chapter 5.
  2. Is the employee count over the 2026-27 threshold described above? If yes, report its net worth. If no, and we own and control it, that guidance excludes it.
  3. Is this a farm we live on? If yes, excluded. If we don’t live on it, report its net worth.
  4. Is this a commercial fishing business we own and control? If yes, excluded, including the related expenses.

Under every one of those, write the same two lines: the year of the guidance you checked, and the date you checked it. Mine for this chapter say 2026-27 and October 2026. Yours should say whatever the published guidance for your student’s award year says on the day you look.

If any answer is “report it” or “I don’t know,” that’s the CPA call, not a second opinion from the internet.

Gabe put the shoebox back in his truck and stood there a second, slightly deflated, the way people get when a thing they’d braced for turns out to be four questions.

“That’s it?”

Four employees, five in spring. Owns it, runs it, excluded. He checked. Next time somebody at the ballfield tells him the rules changed, he’ll be the one who knows which part.

Chapter 5: 529s, Rentals, Crypto and the Assets Nobody Thinks to Report

A family I worked with years ago spent an entire Sunday afternoon arguing about a 529 plan. Not whether to contribute to it. Whether to tell the FAFSA about it at all.

The grandmother had opened it. The mother managed it. The student was the one it was for. Three people, three plausible answers to “whose asset is this,” and not one of them had actually opened the Application and Verification Guide to check.

This chapter is the one where that kind of argument gets settled by a rule instead of a vote. None of what follows is about whether to save for college, or how, or how much. That’s a different book, and this one doesn’t pretend to be it. What follows is only about what the form wants you to report once the saving has already happened.

The 529 question, answered once

Under the 2026-27 Application and Verification Guide, a 529 or Coverdell owned by a parent and designated for this dependent student is reported as a parent asset; an account designated for another child is not included. If a grandparent is the owner and the student is only its named beneficiary, do not report it as the student’s or parent’s asset under that guidance.

Read that twice, because it contains two tests, not one. Designation decides which child the account belongs to: an account someone opened for the student’s younger sibling, or a cousin, or “whoever ends up going to college,” is not reported on this student’s form just because it exists in the same family. Ownership decides whether it lands on the form at all.

The ownership half matters more than people expect. If a grandparent or another non-parent owns the account and the student is only the beneficiary, it is not reported as this student’s or the parent’s asset under the 2026-27 guidance. If a parent owns the account and designated it for this dependent student, report it as a parent asset. That single distinction ends more Sunday-afternoon arguments than almost anything else in this chapter.

It also explains why the family above spent an afternoon arguing past each other. The grandmother was asking an ownership question. The mother was asking a management question. Only the ownership question turns out to matter here.

One line, because this book’s scope stops here: this is a reporting rule, not a planning tip. Whether to put a 529 in a grandparent’s name, a parent’s name, or restructure one before a student applies is a conversation for a financial planner who knows your family’s full picture, not something I’ll walk you through. Check StudentAid.gov for how this treatment applies to the year your student is actually filing.

UGMA and UTMA: the minor’s money, the minor’s asset

A UGMA or UTMA account works differently from a 529, and families sometimes assume the two behave the same way because an adult set both of them up. They don’t.

Under the 2026-27 guidance, a UGMA or UTMA account is the minor’s asset, not the custodian’s, regardless of who manages it or who contributed the money. If your student has one of these accounts in their name, it gets reported as the student’s asset on the student’s side of the form, not folded into the parents’ numbers. That distinction can matter for the arithmetic in ways this book won’t calculate for you until Chapter 7, but the reporting rule itself is simple: it’s the child’s name on the account, so it’s the child’s asset here.

Rental property: the door matters

Families who rent out part of their own home often aren’t sure whether that counts as an investment at all, since it doesn’t feel like the kind of asset the form seems to be asking about.

The 2026-27 guidance draws the line at the unit, not the arrangement. A portion of the home with its own entrance, its own kitchen and its own bath, rented to someone outside the family, is reportable rental property. A bedroom rented to a boarder who shares the kitchen and bathroom with the household is not. The test is physical and specific: can that part of the house function as its own home, separate from the rest of yours, and is the person living there not part of your family.

If you rent out a basement apartment with a lockable door, its own stove and its own shower, report it as an investment under the 2026-27 rule. Then value it carefully, because this is where families overreport. For a qualifying rental unit within your home, first calculate the net value of the entire structure. Then multiply that amount by the fraction represented by the rented unit. Report that portion, not the whole structure’s net value. Ask the school’s aid office or a CPA if you cannot document the fraction.

Net value of the whole structure means the same thing it means everywhere else on this form: current market value minus the debt against it, floored at zero if the subtraction goes negative. The prorating comes after that subtraction, not before it. And the fraction has to be something you could defend to an aid officer who asks: square footage is the usual basis, documented once and kept with the rest of your filing paperwork.

If you rent a spare room to a graduate student who eats breakfast at your table and shares your hallway bathroom, that income may belong elsewhere on your tax return, but it isn’t this kind of reportable asset.

The test doesn’t care whether the arrangement is informal or whether a lease exists on paper. It cares whether the space itself could stand alone as someone else’s home.

Virtual currency: priced the day you file

Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other virtual currency are investments for FAFSA purposes, and the 2026-27 guidance values them in US dollars as of the day the form is completed, not the day you bought them and not some average over the year.

That one detail trips families up because it feels unfair in both directions. A holding that’s up sharply the week you file gets reported at that inflated number, with no averaging to soften it. A holding that’s cratered gets reported low, with no credit for what you paid. The form wants a snapshot, the same way it wants a snapshot of every other investment, and crypto doesn’t get a different rule just because the number moves faster. Price it the day you sit down to file, write down where you got the price, and move on.

Child support received: an asset, not income, and it adds up across the year

Here’s the one that surprises almost every parent who receives it. Child support received is reported as an asset of the recipient, not as income, and the 2026-27 guidance has you total it across every child in the family for the last complete calendar year, then enter the total once.

Parents who’ve been thinking of the monthly deposit as grocery money and school-supply money are sometimes startled to see it land on the asset side of a federal form rather than the income side. It changes nothing about whether you’re entitled to it or how you spend it. It changes where this particular form counts it, and that’s worth knowing before you’re staring at the screen wondering which box it belongs in.

If you’re receiving support for more than one child and the family size on this form includes all of them, add the full year’s total together rather than reporting one child’s share. The number the form wants is the household total for the calendar year the instructions specify, not a per-child breakdown.

Contested ownership: when you genuinely can’t report a number

Separated and divorcing couples sometimes own something jointly that neither one can sell or borrow against without the other’s agreement, and the dispute over it hasn’t resolved by the time the FAFSA is due.

Under the 2026-27 guidance, an asset whose ownership is contested in that way, where you can’t sell it, borrow against it, or otherwise access its value because of the dispute, is not reported while the dispute stands. That’s a narrow exception, built for a specific kind of standoff, not a general escape hatch for anything uncomfortable to value. A house you co-own with an ex-spouse who’s refusing to sign off on a sale or refinance is the kind of situation this covers. A business you’d simply rather not think about valuing is not.

And here’s the part that catches people later: if the dispute resolves after you’ve filed, whether through a settlement, a court order, or the other party finally agreeing, the 2026-27 guidance does not let you go back and update the value on that FAFSA. The snapshot was taken when it was taken. If the resolved value matters to a later award year’s form, it belongs there, filed fresh, not grafted onto an application you already submitted.

If you’re in the middle of exactly this kind of standoff, this is worth a conversation with the attorney handling the separation, not a guess at the kitchen table about how to answer the question.

The exemption that skips the asset questions entirely

Some families don’t answer any of the asset questions in this chapter, because the 2026-27 Application and Verification Guide exempts them from the asset section altogether.

A dependent student qualifies for this exemption if the parents’ base-year combined adjusted gross income is under $60,000 and they filed no Schedule A, B, D, E, F or H. A Schedule C is allowed only if it shows a gain or loss no larger than $10,000. The exemption also applies if the student qualifies for a Maximum Pell Grant on income alone. It applies as well if the student or a parent received a qualifying means-tested federal benefit in either of the two relevant calendar years. Those thresholds and the AGI figure are 2026-27 numbers specifically. Check StudentAid.gov before assuming they carry forward to the year your student is filing.

Three separate doors into the same exemption, in other words. A family only needs to walk through one of them, though one exception closes all three for certain households.

The 2026-27 guide makes an exception: a dependent student is not exempt from asset reporting if the parents live outside the U.S. or do not file taxes in the U.S. or a U.S. territory. Nonfiling because income is below the filing threshold is the exception to that restriction. If this describes your family, ask the aid office what your current-year form requires.

The benefits that trigger that third path, under the same 2026-27 guidance, are the earned income credit, federal housing assistance, free or reduced-price school lunch, Medicaid, the refundable credit for coverage under a qualified health plan, SNAP, SSI, TANF and WIC. Receiving any one of them at any point during either of the two years the instructions specify is enough to qualify. You don’t need to have received all of them, and you don’t need to have received the same one both years.

One item on that list carries a condition most parents miss. For free or reduced-price school lunch, a meal provided through a schoolwide community-eligibility program does not by itself qualify you to check this benefit: under the 2026-27 guide, the household must also meet the USDA income eligibility guidelines. Verify your own award-year instructions before claiming this path.

That distinction matters because community eligibility covers whole schools, not individual households. A family whose child eats free lunch every day because the school qualifies as a building, not because the family qualifies on income, has not met this test. If you aren’t sure which applies to your school, the district’s food services office can tell you in one phone call.

If one of these applies to your family, it’s worth knowing before you sit down to the asset section, because it can mean skipping a set of questions that otherwise cost families the most back-and-forth. It’s also worth confirming on StudentAid.gov rather than assuming from memory, since both the AGI figure and the benefit list are exactly the kind of detail that gets revisited from one award year to the next.

The asset sort

Work through each asset you’re not sure about, one at a time, and sort it into one of three piles.

  1. Reported under the 2026-27 AVG (check the 2027-28 form’s current help before filing): A parent-owned education savings account designated for this dependent student; the student’s UGMA/UTMA; a qualifying separate rental unit, prorated from the home’s net value; virtual currency valued on filing day; and child support received for the calendar year specified by the form.
  2. Excluded under the 2026-27 AVG, subject to the current 2027-28 form instructions: An account designated for a sibling; a non-parent-owned education savings account with this student only as beneficiary; a bedroom sharing the family’s kitchen and bath; or a genuinely contested asset the reporting contributor cannot access. Ask the aid office before omitting an uncertain asset.
  3. Ask the school, or check whether the exemption applies. Anything that doesn’t sit cleanly in the first two piles belongs here. So does a rental fraction you can’t document. So does free lunch you received through a schoolwide program rather than on household income. So does any household where a parent lives abroad or files no U.S. or territory return. And so does anything where your family’s income sits close enough to the exemption’s base-year AGI figure that it’s worth checking before you fill out asset questions you might not need to answer at all.

Most families find that nearly everything they own sorts cleanly into the first two piles once they know the actual tests instead of the family folklore about them. The third pile is small, on purpose. It’s where the genuinely unclear cases belong, and it’s smaller than most parents expect walking in.

The family from the start of this chapter never needed the third pile. Once they knew ownership was the only question that mattered, the grandmother’s account sorted itself, and the argument that had eaten an afternoon took about ninety seconds to settle on a Tuesday night.

Ten minutes. Tonight. Pull up whatever you own that doesn’t obviously belong to the house or the retirement account, and sort it against this list before you ever open the form. Write down the source for each answer — the handbook, the StudentAid.gov page, the date you checked — the same habit Chapter 4 asked of you for the business and farm questions. It takes less time than the argument it prevents.

Chapter 6: Family Size, Who’s Independent, and the Number That Isn’t There Anymore

Rohan pulled another chair toward the kitchen table, then stopped. Anika was at her apartment near campus. We didn’t need the chair. We did need to think about her when we counted our family.

“So next year there are two of us in college,” he said. “That helps, right?”

I wanted to give him the answer he expected. Two tuition bills ought to be noticed somewhere. But noticing a fact and automatically lowering an aid index are different things.

According to the Department’s 2026-27 Federal Student Aid Handbook, the number of family members in college is collected on the FAFSA but isn’t used to calculate the Student Aid Index. SAI, for short. The sibling discount you may remember is not part of that edition’s formula.

The 2026-27 edition of the Application and Verification Guide supplies the administrative rules, through its chapters “Filling Out the FAFSA Form” and “Special Cases.” Check StudentAid.gov for your 2027-28 application. I haven’t inspected authenticated family-size or dependency screens; I won’t invent their wording or click order.

Count people, not chairs

In the 2026-27 guide, family size starts with information from the tax return: the filers plus the dependents, described there as the number of exemptions. This is a count of people, not a tax deduction you’re being asked to calculate.

For online applicants whose required tax permission is supplied and whose information transfers successfully, that handbook describes a shorter task. Family size is derived from the transferred information. The applicant is asked whether the size differs from the tax-return count; a change leads to a follow-up asking for the number of dependents.

Those are 2026-27 mechanics, not a verified description of your 2027-28 screen. Use the current question’s help. The tax-transfer explanation from Chapter 2 supplies the background.

Somebody may have joined the household since the return. A child may no longer meet the support conditions. Don’t answer “unchanged” merely because the income information arrived automatically. Read the current family-size instructions, then compare.

For a dependent student’s family, the 2026-27 guide includes the student, the relevant parent and that parent’s spouse or partner as applicable. The parent selection from Chapter 3 comes first; family size is not an invitation to add the other household back in.

That edition also includes the parent’s dependent children who meet its residence and support conditions. A qualifying temporary absence, including living away for college, does not by itself exclude a child. The required parental support is more than half during July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027, the period named in that handbook. Other people must live with the parent and meet the guide’s support requirements for the entire award year.

Those dates belong to 2026-27. Check StudentAid.gov for your application’s support period and inclusion rules. Don’t shift a date forward and call it verified.

Anika’s empty chair therefore wasn’t the deciding fact. The relevant questions were whether her absence qualified and whether she met the applicable support test. “She’s away at college” isn’t a reason, by itself, to erase her. Nor is “she’s our daughter” a substitute for checking the conditions.

Two students do not divide the index

Family size still matters in the 2026-27 SAI rules. The guide’s chapter on SAI and Pell eligibility identifies it as an input. Number in college does not perform that same role.

Write this beside your notes: family size and college attendance are separate facts.

Don’t divide an index between siblings and call the result their revised aid eligibility. The 2026-27 formula doesn’t do that. Nor should you skip a required college-attendance answer because it doesn’t change the calculation.

For the attendance count, the 2026-27 guide includes the student and qualifying family members enrolled at least half time in a degree or certificate program at a school eligible for federal student aid. A college sweatshirt doesn’t establish enrollment. Check StudentAid.gov for the current definition before counting someone.

The same 2026-27 guide says schools may use the information in a special-circumstances adjustment. Its “Special Cases” chapter specifically names additional family members enrolled in college as a circumstance an administrator may consider. A review is a school decision about documented circumstances, not an automatic sibling reduction.

If overlapping college costs make the family’s finances hard to explain, ask the aid office about its current review process and required records. Don’t promise either child an increase. Use Chapter 10 for the review packet, not a home-made sibling division.

For 2027-28, check StudentAid.gov and the school’s current instructions.

Independent is an aid category, not a compliment

Your student may pay their own phone bill and resent being called dependent. For federal aid, dependency status tells the application whose information is required.

StudentAid.gov’s public “Dependency Status” page, checked October 5, 2026, explains that dependent students report student and parent information. Independent students report their own information and, where applicable, a spouse’s. Dependency does not order a parent to pay tuition.

The tax question is separate. That same Department page says living away from parents or not being claimed on their return does not, alone, establish independence. According to the 2026-27 handbook, reaching age 18 or 21 also does not do it by itself.

You cannot choose an aid status by deciding not to claim your student at tax time. Don’t alter a return on the strength of this book. Use the IRS’s current guidance or a qualified tax preparer for the tax question, and the current FAFSA instructions for the aid question.

A lease isn’t a dependency override. A birthday cake isn’t one either.

Rohan’s age wasn’t permission to skip the other tests.

The independence checklist, with its year attached
