Under the 2026-27 handbook’s overaward guidance, additional assistance can require changes when the package exceeds financial need or attendance cost. That is a packaging review, not permission to lower the school’s stated price yourself.

Ask which lines change and request the revised offer before increasing spending or finalizing borrowing. The effect might include less loan eligibility; institutional adjustments depend on the school’s award policies. No universal dollar-for-dollar outcome belongs here.

For the Pell restriction from Chapter 7: in 2026-27, outside awards that reach the cost of attendance ordinarily bar Pell under Volume 7, except for students qualifying under the Special Rule for certain deceased servicemembers’ or public safety officers’ children. Ask the aid office to check whether it applies and which aid changes; do not assume the same rule for 2027-28.

Report the award either way. Guessing its effect is no substitute for the school evaluating it.

The borrowing order, with a stop condition

Here’s the move. Use this decision checklist beside the amount still unfunded, not as another award-letter sorting sheet.

  1. Confirm available grants and scholarships and report outside awards. Use the package after any required adjustment.
  2. Pursue a workable job. Use earnings only for expenses their timing can cover.
  3. If borrowing remains necessary, consider the student’s offered Direct Subsidized Loan before Direct Unsubsidized borrowing. Request only the needed amount.
  4. Compare parent borrowing separately. Ask the aid office how much Parent PLUS remains available under the rules effective in 2026, and verify the applicable limit at StudentAid.gov, before reading its current obligations against the parent’s budget rather than the student’s hopes.
  5. Consider private borrowing last. Require clear repayment, hardship and cosigner terms, and keep the amount as small as the actual gap permits.

This is an order for evaluating options, not an instruction to use every one. If the gap still requires debt nobody can reasonably carry, stop. Reconsider the attendance plan before adding signatures.

Tonight, open the terms for the next loan you are considering. Find who owes it and when interest starts. Ten minutes to locate those answers. Leave the pen down until you can explain them.

Chapter 12: The Form Is Free. Say It Twice

The mailer looked official enough to leave on the kitchen counter. A neat seal, a photograph of a student in a cap, and one large promise: “We file your FAFSA for you.” The price was $89.

I turned it over. No one at the Department of Education had sent it. The form itself costs nothing to submit. For 2026-27, the Federal Student Aid Handbook prohibited paid preparers; check the current 2027-28 form instructions at StudentAid.gov. In every year, the FAFSA itself is free, and StudentAid.gov warns families not to pay a site to submit it.

That distinction matters. A company may sell general advice about paying for college. A person may help you understand a confusing question. But a fee to prepare or submit the FAFSA is not the same service, and a promise that a payment will secure aid deserves an immediate pause.

The FAFSA is free. Say it twice if the letter is persuasive.

Start at the actual front door

For 2027-28, the form is available through StudentAid.gov. That is the official place to begin, and the Department’s live filling-out page identifies this cycle’s form and its requested tax year. I checked that guidance on October 5, 2026. Use the address you type yourself or a bookmark you made from the official site; don’t let a search advertisement or a mailer choose the destination for you.

Federal Student Aid’s page “Avoiding Student Aid Scams,” also checked October 5, 2026, says the FAFSA is free and directs families to StudentAid.gov. It warns that sites charging to help fill it out are not affiliated with or endorsed by the Department. The page points to free assistance from a college financial aid office, FAFSA online help and the Federal Student Aid Information Center.

The address is a useful first check. The official FAFSA service is on StudentAid.gov. A site with a similar name, an extra word, a different ending or a sponsored search label is not made official by a blue banner or a familiar eagle. Don’t enter personal information just because a page has copied the colors.

If you land somewhere unfamiliar, close it. Open a new browser window, type `StudentAid.gov` yourself, and navigate to the FAFSA from there. You do not need to pay a site to unlock the federal form, send it to a school, or get an application number. If a page asks for a credit card to submit the FAFSA, leave it.

This chapter is not saying every paid service involving college is a fraud. The Federal Student Aid scam page makes that distinction too: charging for advice alone does not prove that a company is fraudulent. What you should not confuse is a paid adviser discussing options with a paid preparer completing the federal form. The FAFSA itself remains free, and the actual filing rules need to be checked on the form for the award year you are using.

What the preparer label does — and doesn’t — mean

I checked Chapter 2 of the Federal Student Aid Handbook for 2026-27: paid preparers are prohibited. In that edition, a Preparer section appears on the paper or PDF form for an unpaid person who completed part of the FAFSA on the applicant’s behalf. That label is not permission for a company to charge for filing. It identifies the unpaid helper in that year’s paper process.

That is a handbook rule for 2026-27, not a claim about what a 2027-28 screen looks like. Check StudentAid.gov for the current form’s instructions and roles. I have not inspected or authenticated a private account screen, so I won’t invent its exact labels or buttons.

An unpaid person can sit beside you, help read a question aloud, or point you to the official explanation. You remain the one who knows whether the answer is true. Each required contributor uses their own StudentAid.gov account to complete and sign their part; don’t hand over a password just because someone offers to type faster. Chapters 1 and 2 cover those steps. Here the point is simpler: assistance with understanding is not ownership of your account.

When an adviser offers a paid package, ask what the fee buys. If it is an optional planning conversation, compare the price and service carefully and remember free help is available. If the person says the fee is for submitting the FAFSA, getting it processed, releasing funds, or securing an award, don’t pay on that claim. Ask the school’s aid office to identify the official step instead.

Never let a preparer put words in your mouth. A false answer remains your family’s problem after the preparer has cashed a check and disappeared. If you don’t know how to answer something, pause and use StudentAid.gov’s help page. Federal Student Aid’s Information Center can also guide you through an unresolved question. A short pause costs less than signing a guess.

The offer that wants money, urgency, or your password

The mailer on the counter had one obvious hook: pay $89 and somebody else would take care of the form. Other messages use different hooks. They may promise a grant that is “already approved,” claim a payment will ensure more aid, or say the family will lose its chance unless a fee is paid right now.

Federal Student Aid’s scam guidance specifically warns about claims of assured aid and pressure to buy immediately. Such a promise is especially slippery: a company might call any offer — including borrowing — proof that it delivered. Chapter 9 showed why the word “aid” on a letter doesn’t tell you whether money is a grant, a loan or wages the student must earn. Don’t let a stranger use that ambiguity to sell certainty.

Another version arrives by phone, text or email. A caller may claim to represent the Department and ask for payment to release the FAFSA, fix a hold or send the application to colleges. The federal form costs nothing to file. Don’t give payment details or personal information to an unexpected caller. Hang up, then contact the school or Federal Student Aid through the contact route you reach from StudentAid.gov, not a number supplied in the message.

Then there’s the request for your FSA ID password. The FSA ID is your StudentAid.gov account sign-in. Federal Student Aid says not to tell anyone the username or password, even someone helping with the FAFSA. The password can be used to access the account and make changes. A real helper can explain a question without taking control of your identity.

Some requests are less theatrical. A website may look nearly right, use a government-sounding name or display a seal. A letter may include your name and a real school. Those details do not verify who sent it. Names and logos are easy to copy; the official domain and a contact method reached independently are better checks.

A three-question pause

Before replying, paying or signing, ask:

  • Is someone charging specifically to prepare or submit the FAFSA, or promising that a fee will secure aid?
  • Is anyone asking for a StudentAid.gov username or password, payment details, or a one-time verification code?
  • Is the message pushing you to act immediately while asking you to use its link or callback number?

A yes is a stop sign, not a reason to negotiate. It doesn’t prove every company that sells general financial-aid advice is fraudulent; it means you should verify what the service is, what the fee covers, and whether the federal filing remains yours. For FAFSA submission, return to StudentAid.gov. For an account or aid question, use the contact links at that site to find the school or Federal Student Aid staff.

Keep the message, envelope, receipt or screenshot if you think you were misled. Don’t forward it to a stranger who claims to investigate. Use the reporting directions on StudentAid.gov’s “Avoiding Student Aid Scams” page. If money has already left your account, contact your bank or card issuer using the number on its official card or website and ask what options apply. A payment dispute does not mean the money will be returned; describe exactly what was promised and delivered.

If someone already has your password

No scolding. Fix access first.

Go directly to StudentAid.gov by typing the address. Follow the current account-security instructions to change the password and review the account’s contact details. Federal Student Aid’s scam guidance tells people whose FSA ID information has been shared to change the password. If you cannot get into the account or see contact information you did not add, contact the Federal Student Aid Information Center through StudentAid.gov’s Help Center. Don’t use a link from the person who had the password.

Tell your student and any other contributor who may be affected. Each person protects their own account; one password change does not secure a different contributor’s login. If an application was changed or submitted without your agreement, contact the school’s financial aid office and ask what it can see, what records it needs, and how to correct the situation. Use the school’s secure method for documents. Do not send passwords or full account credentials in an email.

If you shared a password with a paid preparer, change it even if the person seems trustworthy. If they only helped read a question and never had the password, there may be nothing to repair. Keep the distinction plain; panic makes every kind offer look like a threat and every threat look like a kind offer.

If you paid a company but did not share a password, keep the contract, advertisement, messages and proof of payment. Contact the company only through contact details you verify independently if you need to request a refund or records. If it claimed to be the Department, charged to submit the FAFSA, or did not provide the promised service, use StudentAid.gov’s reporting guidance and consider contacting the Federal Trade Commission. A fee for advice is not automatically fraud; describe the facts rather than applying a label you can’t support.

The help that is real

You can get help without surrendering the form. StudentAid.gov provides online FAFSA help. A college’s financial aid office can answer questions about its process and its own aid. The Federal Student Aid Information Center handles federal application and account questions. Those routes are free; start from StudentAid.gov or the school’s official website so you know whom you reached.

A tax preparer may help with the family’s tax return. That is a different job from charging to prepare or submit the FAFSA. If you are unsure which tax-year information belongs on the form, or the return itself may need correction, take the tax question to your preparer or a certified public accountant. The aid office can help with the form, not amend a tax return. For the FAFSA field, use StudentAid.gov’s explanation or ask the aid office. Don’t ask one professional to make a claim outside their role.

And help does not mean someone else should make a contributor’s account, supply the contributor’s consent, or sign as that person. Chapter 2 separated those actions. Keep the password private, answer from the records you have, and ask about a question you cannot resolve. A competent helper will leave you in control.

A small check before you close the envelope

Here’s the move. If a message or mailer offers to handle FAFSA, set it beside your computer and check three things before doing anything:

  1. Go to StudentAid.gov by typing the address yourself. Confirm you’re using the official federal form, not a look-alike service.
  2. Read what the person is actually charging for. Advice is not the same as preparing or submitting the FAFSA; a promise of assured aid is not evidence.
  3. Keep your account credentials to yourself. If they were shared, change the password using the official account route and contact the Information Center if access is uncertain.

Write the provider’s name, the exact promise, the fee and the date on the back of the mailer. If any piece is vague, don’t sign or pay yet. Call the financial aid office or the Information Center from a contact page you opened yourself. You do not need to decide while the caller is waiting on the line.

The process can be long and still be legitimate. A slow page is not evidence that an $89 service can fix it. Each contributor who completes their own section, provides required permission and signs through the proper route has done the work the application asks of them. If something looks wrong, stop and verify it at the official source.

Put the mailer in the recycling, or keep it if you need its details to report. Then open a fresh browser window and start at StudentAid.gov. Ten minutes. Tonight.

A Form, Not a Test

Rohan had his elbow on the yellow pad beside the fruit bowl. The laptop was open. He was reading, not typing, and his free hand kept finding the edge of the lid.

“I still don’t like this,” he said.

I had promised to sit beside him while we worked out what it was asking. There were still questions on our pad, and college still cost more than either of us wanted it to. But he could tell me which part had stopped him. The first evening, one unfamiliar word had sent him out the door.

He wasn’t suddenly calm. He was further along.

You may recognize that table. No delighted family holding a perfect award letter. No assurance that enough money will arrive because you were careful. A parent and a student who can stay with the page long enough to understand the question. Some evenings, that is quite a bit.

The questions arrived one at a time. So did the answers. What had looked like one enormous decision became the next question on the page.

You don’t have to recite that route. Nothing about recognizing an acronym on sight makes you a better parent. I’d rather you understood the sentence in front of you than remembered every abbreviation in these pages. We don’t need to make a family spelling bee out of them.

The important difference at our table was that a question could now be small. It could be about one account, one line in an offer, one fact we needed to confirm. Before, every unknown had seemed to contain the whole college decision. Where would he go? Could we pay? Had we already ruined something? All of that crowded into the space beside a single field.

The worries didn’t disappear when the field made sense. They did stop pretending to be the same worry.

You may still have a form in progress. You may have an offer you understand and a price you cannot comfortably meet. Reading to this page doesn’t tell me which. I won’t write your family’s result into the blank space. Understanding a cost is not the same as having the money, and a clear explanation doesn’t make an uncomfortable answer pleasant.

I don’t like advice that treats a parent’s worry as a failure of attitude. If the amount left to pay is beyond you, confidence isn’t a payment source. If a family circumstance is complicated, a cheerful sentence doesn’t settle it. You can be careful and still face a hard choice. That doesn’t mean the careful work was wasted. It means you can see the choice without a misleading label covering it.

Recognizing the debt didn’t decide whether the family could manage it. That was why the borrowing discussion needed its own space after the offer. I would distrust a book that chose for you without knowing the bills on your kitchen counter.

Where the handbook edition was older than this application cycle, I named it rather than quietly changing the year. The official sources throughout the book remain the places for current instructions. No missing figure appears here to make the story feel complete. An unanswered question is more useful than an answer borrowed from the wrong year.

Saving for college and choosing a 529 investment strategy remain outside this book; the IRS’s “Qualified tuition programs” page and your state’s plan information are starting places for that separate subject.

And the professional-help promise from the opening still stands. When your school’s offer needs explanation or your circumstances need its review, the school’s aid office is the place to call. Federal Student Aid names that office as a source of free help in “Avoiding Student Aid Scams”; its “Filling Out the FAFSA Form” guidance places changed-finances decisions with the school. I checked both on October 5, 2026. For a change to that school’s offer, the authority is there, not with me. You aren’t supposed to become an aid administrator to ask for help from one.

I know the urge to apologize before asking. You have read something twice and still cannot tell what it means. You imagine the person answering has heard the question all day. At the front counter, I much preferred a parent who could say where they were stuck to one who nodded and left with an answer they hadn’t understood. I could explain a form. I could not know what silence meant.

That old habit followed me home. I had to remember it when the parent at the table was me. Being able to explain a word didn’t give me authority over the outcome, and being worried didn’t make me unfit to ask a question.

Rohan moved his elbow. The pad had a crease through the line we’d been discussing. He smoothed it with his palm and looked back at the screen. I left the laptop within his reach, rather than pulling it toward me to hurry things along.

He read the sentence again. Then he pointed to the words he didn’t understand.

This time, he stayed.
